claims.text: Multicomponent high-entropy alloys can exist in both solid and liquid states at or near their high melting temperatures.
Replacing an EAM reference with an actively trained machine-learning interatomic potential will significantly improve reference–target phase-space overlap.
The proposed MLIP will be iteratively refined using ab initio liquid configurations selected through active learning.
Sampling a broad spectrum of liquid configurations during training will enable the MLIP to represent configurations missed by conventional EAM references.
The applicable temperature window is roughly within ±100 °C of the alloy's high melting point.
The method is intended for conditions where solid and liquid phases coexist or are in equilibrium.
Higher-order atomic descriptors can resolve many-body interactions in these multicomponent alloys.
Higher-order descriptors will capture local distortions typical of the ab initio liquid.
Capturing many-body interactions and liquid local distortions will produce a smoother energy landscape between the reference and target systems.
Training on diverse liquid-phase ab initio data will improve representation of the target configuration space relative to fixed-form EAM potentials.
Improved configuration-space representation will expand phase-space overlap between the reference and ab initio target systems.
Greater reference–target phase-space overlap will produce a smoother and shorter thermodynamic-integration path.
The MLIP reference will reduce thermodynamic-integration path mismatch by approximately 40–50% relative to TOR-TILD EAM references.
Reduced path mismatch will lead to more accurate free-energy predictions.
TOR-TILD uses EAM-based reference potentials.
TOR-TILD's EAM references lack sufficient flexibility to represent the full diversity of configurations in an ab initio liquid.
The anticipated improvement applies primarily to compositions similar to those represented in the MLIP training set.
Performance may degrade for compositions or temperatures far outside the MLIP calibration range.
The magnitude of mismatch reduction depends on the quality and diversity of the ab initio training data.
Failure to achieve at least an approximately 40% reduction in a specified path-mismatch metric relative to the EAM control would falsify the hypothesis.
